summary: Seed A1 and B1 are compatible accounts of SQLite's documented reader end-mark constraint on a single PASSIVE checkpoint. A2 and B2 are compatible but untested scheduling extensions about omitted reader lifecycle and release timing. Retrieved Walack prior work rules out novelty claims for general read/write-aware adaptive checkpoint frequency. No new representation or experiment is justified at this stage.

artifacts.description: Bridge synthesis of seed explanations, retrieved sources, known mechanisms, and a staged measurable contrast.
Prior single-run local SQLite probe; 143/143 checkpointed frames without a held reader and 2/143 with one, at equal WAL bytes and busy=0. Not a bridge-stage experiment.
Completed Seed A retry proposals A1/A2; the original Seed A attempt timed out.
Completed independent Seed B proposals B1/B2.

evidence.details: SQLite 3.51.3; one run per condition; same 2400 rows, 143 log frames, 589192 WAL bytes, and busy=0; checkpointed frames were 143 without a held reader and 2 with a held reader.

OpenAlex work W4393207694 plus Crossref DOI metadata/abstract. Abstract identifies SQLite WAL and describes asynchronous fsync plus checkpoint-frequency adjustment from observed read/write requests; full paper not retrieved.

PostgreSQL 18 docs describe MVCC vacuum reclaiming obsolete versions only when they are no longer visible to transactions; long-running transactions are relevant to cleanup and wraparound recovery. Analogy only.
SQLite WAL documentation states that reader end marks can limit checkpoint progress. Live page retrieval succeeded; the project also has a verified local copy.
Project's verified copy documents PASSIVE behavior and log/checkpointed frame counters.

claims: A1/B1 are compatible and largely restate a documented SQLite mechanism; the seed observation is directionally consistent but does not vary snapshot position or replicate.

A2/B2 ask the same open scheduling question at different emphasis: whether reader lifecycle/release timing adds actionable information beyond matched aggregate telemetry. Neither has evidence of an observability boundary or policy benefit.

Walack is direct prior work for asynchronous and read/write-aware adaptive checkpoint frequency. Novelty cannot be claimed for that general idea; precise overlap with SQLite reader end-mark scheduling remains unresolved without full-text review.
PostgreSQL MVCC vacuum is a cross-domain analogue of maintenance constrained by active transaction visibility, not evidence of equivalent mechanics or a new SQLite representation.
limitations: No scientific experiment was run in this stage, as instructed.
Walack full text was not retrieved; only OpenAlex record and Crossref abstract/metadata were reviewed.
The scout has one run per condition and cannot establish a causal or performance effect.
No held-out workload, matched telemetry history, independent evidence of policy-visible reader age, or strategy comparison exists.
next_actions: First replicate the immediate end-mark contrast on fresh databases, matching SQLite build, writes, commit boundaries, WAL head, and PASSIVE action while varying only reader snapshot prefix; randomize order and report frame counts.

If replicated, freeze policy-visible signals and compare fixed-period, WAL-size, and request-rate triggers with an explicitly available reader-age/history signal on held-out release/burst traces; treat actual future releases as diagnostic only.
Count calls/time and completed work, and report residual WAL work plus reader completion and commit tail latency; do not infer a strategy gain from frame counts alone.
Review Walack full text and its cited work before making any literature-gap or novelty claim.

sources.relation: SQLite reader end-mark mechanism; directly explains the shared A1/B1 idea and is known prior behavior.
Defines PASSIVE checkpoint behavior and frame-count outputs used by proposed measurements.
Walack is a direct prior baseline for asynchronous, read/write-aware adaptive WAL checkpoint frequency; full text not reviewed.
Cross-domain MVCC vacuum analogy: transaction visibility constrains when old versions can be reclaimed; transfer to SQLite checkpointing is limited.
